title: Next Bigger Number With the Same Digits
statement:
You get a positive integer n. Rearrange its digits to form the smallest number that is strictly greater than n, using every digit exactly as many times as it appears in n.

Return that number. Return -1 if no rearrangement is bigger, or if the smallest bigger one does not fit in a signed 32-bit integer (greater than 2 147 483 647).

examples.why: Only the 2 can grow: the smallest larger digit to its right is 3. Then the rest, 2, 6, 7, goes in ascending order.
Digits in descending order are already the largest arrangement.
The next arrangement is 9199999999, which is above 2 147 483 647.

hints: To get the next larger number, change the rightmost possible digit, so the change is as small as possible. Which digit can you increase using only digits to its right?
Scan from the right. As long as digits go up as you move left, that suffix is already at its maximum. The first digit that is smaller than the one to its right is the pivot.
Swap the pivot with the smallest digit in the suffix that is still larger than it. The suffix stays descending, so reversing it makes it the smallest possible. Then check the 32-bit limit.

explain.intuition:
A suffix whose digits go down from left to right, like …763, is already the biggest arrangement of those digits. To get anything larger you must touch the digit just before it, the pivot. To make the increase as small as possible, swap the pivot with the smallest suffix digit that beats it, and then arrange the suffix as small as possible.

After the swap the suffix is still in descending order, so reversing it gives ascending order: the smallest arrangement. This is exactly the "next permutation" step. The only extra is the 32-bit limit: build the answer as a number and compare it with 2 147 483 647.
steps: Find the largest i with d[i] < d[i + 1]. If none exists, return -1.
Find the largest j > i with d[j] > d[i] and swap d[i] and d[j].
Convert back; return it if it is at most 2 147 483 647, else -1.
pitfalls: Swapping with the first larger digit found from the left of the suffix instead of the smallest larger one: 2763 would become 7263 instead of 3267.
Using a strict comparison where the scan should step over equal digits. In 1550 the pivot is the 1, not a 5.
Forgetting the overflow check. Ten-digit inputs can produce valid arrangements above the 32-bit limit.

complexity.time: O(d), d = number of digits (at most 10)

solutions.title: Pivot, pick, sort the tail
solutions.idea: Find the pivot, swap in the smallest larger digit from its right, then sort the remaining tail ascending.

solutions.title: Next permutation in place
solutions.idea: Same pivot. The suffix is descending, so the last digit larger than the pivot is the smallest larger one, and reversing the suffix sorts it.

followups: Return the next smaller number with the same digits instead. Which comparisons flip?
